newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy economy slack, employers grumble at govt.
newsitem.headline: Italy economy slack, employers grumble at govt.

text.p: The Italian economy slowed even more than expected in 1996, national statistics office ISTAT said on Friday, and industrialists warned that the government's latest budget package would make make matters worse.

ISTAT said Italy's gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.7 percent last year against preliminary data which pointed to a 0.8 percent increase. GDP grew 2.9 percent in 1995, revised down from a previously given three percent.

The data were released the day after Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government approved a 15.5 trillion lire ($9.3 billion) mini-budget in a final bid to get state accounts ready for the single European currency.

Much of the package was based on fiscal and accountancy changes and included a demand that firms hand over six trillion lire this year and a similar amount in 1998 in advance taxes on severance funds, which are set aside to pay departing workers.
"Companies are becoming blood donors, but I don't know if we've got much more to give," said industrialist Luigi Orlando, chairman of metalwork company SMI.

Employers' federation Confindustria said late on Thursday it would call an emergency meeting of all its members for April 10 to discuss how to fight the package -- the first time the group has called such an assembly.
The organisation stressed in a statement its "strongest opposition to the corrective package...which contains further oppressive measures for business.
"It will further depress the construction sector, which is already in crisis. It makes no provision for structural spending cuts and will generate more unemployment," it added.

ISTAT said earlier this week that the jobless rate hit 12.4 percent of the work force in January against 12.2 percent last October -- the highest level since new counting methods were introduced in 1992.
But the statistics office on Friday said the number of people in work actually rose 0.2 percent in 1996, the first increase seen in four years.

It added that 1996 GDP was boosted by 2.4 percent growth in agriculture output and a 1.8 percent increase in the construction sector. On the downside, the industrial and energy sectors fell 0.4 percent and 0.7 percent respectively.
ISTAT's director general Paolo Garonno said the economy had been hurt by lira gains last year, which caused a 0.3 percent drop in exports, in terms of volumes, after an 11.6 percent surge in 1995.
The government has predicted GDP growth of 1.2 percent this year and Prodi said the mini-budget, needed to plug a hole in Treasury coffers, would not damage the economy.
"It protects the interests of the weak and does not upset prospects for development," Prodi told reporters on Thursday.
But firms warned that their costs would rise if they had to find 12 trillion lire in advance taxes over the next two years, meaning investment would be stunted.
